notes: A running account of where things stand by these headlines, revised after each edition rather than added to. Every version is kept.
Written by the model from the narratives, not from the headlines. It is a reading, not a record.
standing: Brent crude reached $117.64 on 31 October as the war with Iran went on, Italy's inflation rose to 5.4% with its president blaming stagnant wages, Colombia, Nigeria and Vietnam opened minimum or public pay rounds, and Turkey, Germany and Japan argued over fuel and consumption tax relief. A US technology sell-off over AI spending deepened, with Alphabet's biggest fall on record, Intel down 29% in a day and the Nasdaq on course for a $2 trillion October loss, while Taiwan, reporting its fastest growth in fifty years, saw nearly a trillion Taiwan dollars of foreign selling in a month and its state funds and central bank buying. European ministers shunned Sergei Lavrov at the G20, while US and Russian foreign ministers talked at APEC, Washington weighed lifting sanctions on a Putin associate and approved 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine, and Russia signed 53 documents at its Africa summit. Protests called for the weekend of 31 October were banned in La Rochelle, allowed within perimeters in Rochefort and Saintes, and negotiated in Lisbon, with more than 150,000 young Germans signed up and arrests threatened outside the US embassy in London. Brazil's contested count, the US midterm lawsuits, drones, Yoon Suk Yeol's case and the Urda rail collision had no narrative today.
moved: The Iran and fuel thread turned back within a day. The 30 October reading of Washington pressing the oil price down gave way on 31 October to Brent up 2.4% at $117.64 and the war's price rise argued over in Italian inflation, pay rounds in three countries and tax relief in three more.

The AI spending thread became a sell-off and reached public money: Alphabet's record fall, Intel's 29% drop and a $2 trillion Nasdaq loss for October, with Taiwan's state funds and central bank buying against record foreign selling.
A new thread began on Russia, shunned by European ministers at the G20 while Washington and African governments negotiate and trade with it.

The students thread, silent since 27 October, was revived as protests called for the same weekend across Europe, met with a ban in La Rochelle, perimeters in Rochefort and Saintes and negotiation in Lisbon.
silent: Brazil's election and the United States is now silent, with no narrative since the evening of 27 October. Its events ran under other threads on 29 and 30 October, but none appeared on 31 October, so this may be the story going quiet after Flávio Bolsonaro's exit as much as the sample.

Public schemes falling short, AI fakes in checks and removals over offence, all begun on the evening of 27 October, have gone three editions without a narrative and are silent. Each was a single observation and may simply not have been a strong join since.

The single observations from 26 and 27 October remain silent. Halloween falls on 31 October, but the only trace of it was the price of Halloween sweets inside the wage narrative, so the rites thread has not returned.

threads.label: Iran war, oil prices, borrowing and wages
threads.text: On 26 October the join was the Gulf running talks and strike preparations side by side. On 27 October it was the Hormuz shock at the pump, then jet fuel, Estonian asphalt and subsidies in Malaysia, India, Ukraine and South Korea. On 29 October it reached borrowing, with the Fed holding and South Korean mortgage rates at a 14-year high. On 30 October reports ran the other way: Washington pressing Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries, a US peace proposal to Tehran and US mortgage rates down. On 31 October Brent rose 2.4% to $117.64, Italy's inflation reached 5.4%, Colombia, Nigeria and Vietnam opened pay rounds, and Turkey, Germany and Japan argued over tax relief. The edition's case against says only Italy's figure and the fuel relief clearly carry the oil price.
threads.direction: After a one-day reading of easing on 30 October, it has returned to the war's price rise spreading outward, now from tax receipts towards wages.

threads.label: Brazil's election and the United States
threads.text: On 26 October Brazil's vote was read as a script in Buenos Aires, Madrid and Nairobi. On the morning of 27 October Trump called the election rigged; by that evening, after Lula's run-off win, the United States was the common party in Flávio Bolsonaro's exit, Lula's warning of persecution, about 300 US soldiers in Colombia and Machado's return to Venezuela. Its events then ran under wider joins: Flávio Bolsonaro's arrival in the United States and an amnesty plan for Jair Bolsonaro on 29 October, and Flávio's letter declaring himself president on 30 October. Nothing from Brazil appeared on 31 October, and the thread is now silent.
threads.direction: It moved from how Brazil's vote is read abroad to Washington's part in what follows, then was taken up under wider joins and fell silent.

threads.label: AI companies' listing, land and lawsuits
threads.text: On 26 October the join was an AI company listing the end of the world as a risk factor in its prospectus and the market buying the shares. Early on 27 October an edition followed data centres to county level, where land, grid and water requests were refused, and that morning Anthropic filed for a record US share listing as Elvis Presley's rights holders sued it over 200 songs. Data centres split into their own thread on 29 October. No narrative on listings or lawsuits has followed in four editions; the share falls of Alphabet and Intel on 30 and 31 October were carried in the data centre thread.
threads.direction: It went from the prospectus to the ground and the courts, then fell silent as its market side was carried under the data centre thread.

threads.label: Young people's protests and their policing
threads.text: On 26 October the join was young people in public squares, with students bringing down a government. On the morning of 27 October students were on strike or occupying buildings in France, Mexico, India and Italy. After three editions without a narrative, the Chronicle revived it on 31 October, when protests called for the same weekend met different answers: La Rochelle banned gatherings on the 31st while Rochefort and Saintes set perimeters, Lisbon's police set no red lines for Rossio, Hague shops braced for a 'Gen Z protest', over 150,000 young Germans signed up and arrests were threatened outside the US embassy in London. The edition marked it tentative and found no common organiser or demand; the revival is the Chronicle's judgment, as the narrative cited no earlier one.
threads.direction: It has moved from youth as a political image, to named student strikes, to how states police one weekend's crowds.

threads.label: State housing drives and housing protests
threads.text: On the morning of 27 October one narrative joined Egypt, Indonesia and Tamil Nadu expanding housing through states and employers with Portugal investigating police conduct at housing protests, and the part property funds play. No narrative has followed it in four editions. Mortgage rates appeared in the oil thread on 29 and 30 October, and on 31 October Lisbon's housing camps and the Rossio demonstration appeared in the revived protest thread.

threads.label: Public schemes passing costs to households
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. In six countries a public scheme meant to cover a cost was reported as falling short: Canadians paying for private surgery from savings and GoFundMe, German adult children billed for parents' care, Lucknow's subsidised generic pharmacies short of medicines, a Bangladeshi antivenom programme lacking funds, compensation claims from 50,000 Australians over unlawful Centrelink suspensions, and doubt over a Mexican voluntary pension scheme. The case against noted that several of these stories have run for years. No narrative has carried it in the three editions since, and it is now silent.

threads.label: AI-made faces and files in checks
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. Nigeria's electoral commission is investigating suspected AI-generated photos in the voters' register, New Zealand job seekers report being ignored as AI-written applications flood employers, an Australian court passed the first sentence under deepfake laws without jail, and fashion models face AI copies of their image. The join is that a plausible picture or document now costs little to make while checking it still takes a person's time. No narrative has carried it in the three editions since, and it is now silent.

threads.label: Broadcasts and films removed over offence
threads.text: Begun on the evening of 27 October. A Chinese platform dropped Racing-Real Madrid and La Liga broadcasts were suspended after a remark by Mbappé, an Indian court ordered a documentary on Adani and Modi taken down, a Korean drama faced calls to halt over a Gwangju episode, and Neil Young sued to stop Trump rallies using his songs. Three of the headlines were the same Mbappé story. No narrative has carried it in the three editions since, and it is now silent.

threads.label: AI spending: profit, dispute and sell-off
threads.text: Begun on 29 October with Samsung and CHPT profits on AI data centre demand alongside a Norwegian freeze proposal, a Finnish forest police report and attacks on Russian data centres. On 30 October it reached US growth of 3.4% credited to AI investment and the results of Amazon and Alphabet. On 31 October the markdown deepened: Alphabet had its biggest fall on record, Intel lost 29% in a day and the Nasdaq is on course for a $2 trillion October loss. Taiwan, reporting its fastest growth in fifty years, saw nearly a trillion Taiwan dollars of foreign selling in a month while its state funds and central bank bought. The case against says Taiwan's fund buys in most large sell-offs and Intel's fall is its own. No planning dispute has appeared since 29 October.
threads.direction: It has moved from profit and local objection to national growth, then to a share sell-off whose losses are partly taken on by Taiwanese public money.

threads.label: Former leaders between courts and amnesty
threads.text: Begun on 29 October. South Korea's special counsel again sought, and by one report won, a death sentence for former president Yoon Suk Yeol over his martial law declaration, while in Brazil Alcolumbre planned a pardon or amnesty for Jair Bolsonaro and Flávio Bolsonaro reached the United States with Trump's consent. An expert report contradicted Spain's Zapatero over jewels, India seized Azam Khan's university and Indonesia's parliament opened its anti-corruption law to revision. On 30 October Flávio Bolsonaro's letter appeared in the contested-count thread; no narrative carried the court cases on 30 or 31 October, and one more edition without it turns it silent.

threads.label: Failed safety systems and operator blame
threads.text: Begun on 29 October and marked tentative by its own edition. A high-speed collision near Urda in Spain, which other headlines say killed 68 people, followed at least 15 warnings about faulty signalling; a JR train in Japan overran a station when its driver was drowsy and its automatic braking did not act; Bangladesh is investigating a grid failure and an identity server outage; Manila's airport has broken CCTVs; and Mexico lost internet across several networks. Only the Spanish and Japanese cases have a stated cause. No narrative carried it on 30 or 31 October; one more edition without it and it turns silent.

threads.label: Vote counts and rolls as contested ground
threads.text: Begun on 30 October. Flávio Bolsonaro released a letter declaring himself president of Brazil and then left the country; in Israel, Gadi Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of trying to delegitimise a result that gave no bloc a majority; in the United States, days before the midterms, a federal inquiry into the Alaska vote is widening and Texas's attorney general is suing Houston's county clerk; in Delhi BJP booth agents filed deletion forms against Muslim voters; and in Imo, Nigeria, a governorship is disputed. The case against notes that it sets a coup attempt beside a suit over voter adverts. No narrative carried it on 31 October, though the midterms are still days away.

threads.label: Drones in war, numbers and arms production
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined drones cutting power, guarding a lake, carrying the wounded and being sold. It was silent for three editions. On 30 October drones returned as a matter of numbers: Ukrainian commanders describe a shortage of interceptors against jet-powered drones, a record raid shut airports in Moscow and St Petersburg, Finland trains soldiers against drones, Ukraine's central bank eases loans to arms makers and Lithuania will conscript all men from 2032. The revival was the Chronicle's judgment, as the 30 October narrative cited no earlier one. No narrative carried drones on 31 October, though Washington's approval of 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine appeared in the new Russia thread.
threads.direction: It has moved from the drone's many uses to the number of drones and the factories and conscripts states are raising to match them.

threads.label: Russia shunned by Europe, courted elsewhere
threads.text: Begun on 31 October. European ministers refused to stand beside Sergei Lavrov for the G20 photograph and Poland's foreign minister told him 'enough', while US and Russian foreign ministers discussed coordination at APEC, Washington weighed lifting sanctions on a Putin associate, Russia signed 53 documents at its Africa summit and Nigeria moved to replace a 1967 air agreement with Moscow. Washington also approved 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine. The case against says the Europeans still attended, Europe has a role in the Abu Dhabi talks, and the African deals renew old ties. It sits close to the 30 October report, carried in the oil thread, that Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries under Trump's pressure.

threads.label: Money leaving and states offering discounts
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative joined savings and fortunes moving into dollars, gold and trusts with states answering by amnesties and discounts meant to bring the money back into view. No narrative in the five editions since has followed it, so it stands as a single observation. The amnesty bills of 29 October concern convictions, not tax or hidden money.

threads.label: AI buyouts and dangerous manual work
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative set office workers being paid to leave as AI takes their tasks against labourers still dying in ditches, fields and collapsed buildings. No later narrative has carried it in five editions. AI has appeared since as fakes, data centres, national growth and a share sell-off, but not as a matter of jobs; wages appeared on 31 October only through the oil price.

threads.label: Rites counted before the days of the dead
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative joined reports that measured the rites of late October and early November before they happen: numbers of hosts, incense sticks, costumes and the strain on worshippers' knees. No narrative has carried it in the five editions since. On 31 October, Halloween itself, the only trace was a headline on the rising cost of Halloween sweets inside the wage narrative. The days of the dead on 1 and 2 November are still ahead.

threads.label: European household readiness and borrowed deterrence
threads.text: Early on 27 October one narrative joined European advice that households should be able to last 72 hours on their own with European states seeking cover from nuclear warheads they do not own. No narrative in the five editions since has returned to it. Finnish anti-drone training and Lithuanian conscription on 30 October went to the drones thread, and Europe's stance towards Russia on 31 October to a new thread.

threads.label: One football night watched worldwide
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined coverage of a single football night that drew attention across many countries at once. It was tied to one event and no narrative has carried it in the six editions since. Football returned on 27 October only as a broadcasting dispute in the removal-over-offence thread.

threads.label: Courts re-sentencing past events
threads.text: On 26 October one narrative joined courts re-sentencing events of 1979 and 1996 with a library removing material from 2026, treating them as revisions of the record. No narrative has carried it in the six editions since. The former-leaders and contested-count threads touch nearby ground, but neither re-sentences an old event.

withdrawn.held: AI companies' share listings, the copyright suit against Anthropic and county refusals of data centre land, grid and water formed one thread.
withdrawn.undone: On 29 October data centres returned on their own, as profit for Samsung and CHPT and as planning and security disputes in Norway, Finland and Russia, with no listing or lawsuit in view. The land and power question is running apart from the companies' finance and courts, so the merge no longer holds.

withdrawn.held: The Iran war's price rise was moving outward from the pump to central bank rates and loan contracts, with the war named less often at each step.
withdrawn.undone: On 30 October the reports ran the other way: Washington pressing Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries and sending Tehran a peace proposal, Israel's pump price set to fall, Russia budgeting on $50 oil and US mortgage rates down for two weeks. The war was named directly again, and the costs were reported as easing more than spreading.

withdrawn.held: The data centre question was running apart from the AI companies' finance, as a matter of land, power and security.
withdrawn.undone: On 30 October the data centre thread itself turned to finance: US growth credited to AI investment, Amazon's spending and Alphabet's fall in market value, with no planning or security dispute in that edition. The split of threads stands, but the separation of data centres from company finance does not.

withdrawn.held: On 30 October the Iran war's costs had turned towards easing, with Washington pressing for a lower oil price before the midterms.
withdrawn.undone: On 31 October Brent rose 2.4% to $117.64, Italy's inflation reached 5.4% and the price rise was argued over in pay rounds and tax relief in several countries. The easing reading did not last a day, and the earlier withdrawal of the outward-spread reading now looks premature.

caseAgainst: This Chronicle rests on seven editions over about 98 hours, still with none stamped 28 October. Two of today's four narratives carry continuation links, and the brief that asks for continuity may produce them as much as the world does. The oil thread has now been read as spreading, then easing, then spreading again in three consecutive versions; that swing may say more about which headlines each collection caught than about the oil market, and I have withdrawn readings on single editions twice. The wage join rests firmly only on Italy's inflation figure and the fuel relief schemes, as its own case against says. The sell-off falls in US earnings week at the end of a month, and Taiwan's fund buys in most large falls. The Russia thread rests on a G20, an APEC meeting and an Africa summit in the same week, so the meetings calendar may have made the pattern. Reviving the students thread was my judgment on a tentative narrative gathered on the eve of one weekend, with no common organiser named. My earlier versions led with the war, and I have led with it again.
line: On 31 October 2026, with Brent at $117.64, the Iran war's price rise reaches wage talks, and Taiwan's state funds buy as a US tech sell-off over AI spending deepens.
revision: The Brazil, public schemes, AI fakes and removal-over-offence threads are marked silent; a new thread on Russia was begun and the students thread revived around one weekend's protests, leaving eight live. The 30 October reading of easing war costs is withdrawn after Brent rose and the price rise reached pay rounds, and the standing was rewritten around oil and wages, the AI sell-off and Taiwan, Russia and the weekend protests.
